Materials in Doppio: procedural library, real depth and baking

Stable Doppio Last updated: 2026-11-18

A practical guide to authoring tileable PBR materials with the procedural node library, depth and map baking.

Looking for sprites, leaves, flames or packed VFX masks instead of a PBR material? That is the separate Texture Generator: see texture-generator-guide.md.

This guide covers what you need to author realistic, tileable PBR materials without downloading third-party assets: the procedural node library, the preset library, the Output node, parallax depth and how baking works. Images are rendered by the engine itself and captured headless; the commands to regenerate them are at the end.

1. The procedural library#

The Generator tab is a node graph that bakes into the material's maps. Besides the original nodes it now has 129 data-driven operations (uikit/procedural/), all seeded, tileable and multi-threaded:

Category Examples
Noise (16) Perlin / Simplex-like / Value FBM, Ridged, Billow, Turbulence, Worley variants, Domain-warped, Clouds, Gabor-like
Natural (17) Dirt, Scratches, Cracks, Rust, Moss, Strata, Sand ripples, Wood grain, Marble veins, Leather pores, Brushed metal, Caustics
Patterns (18) Tiles, Hex tiles, Bricks (running bond), Herringbone, Basket weave, Stripes, Rings, Scales, Cobblestones, Planks, Diamond plate, Perforated, Knurl
Shapes (8) Linear / radial / angular / diamond gradients, Circle, Rectangle, Polygon, Star
Math (25) Add, Multiply, Lerp, Remap, Clamp, Power, Smoothstep, Posterize, Gradient Map, Channel Split/Merge…
Geometry (8) Transform 2D, Mirror, Polar, Twirl, Pixelate, Slope Blur, Tile Sampler, Warp
Height & PBR (14) Height-to-Normal, Height Blend, Terrace, Bevel, Curvature, multi-scale AO, Edge Wear, Dust
Variation (6) Noise Variation, Cell Variation, Patch Blend, Tile Shuffle, Wave Function Collapse, Diamond-Square
Realistic (17) Rock Fracture, River Pebbles, Grass Blades, Water Waves, Foam, Bark Fissures, Soil Clumps, Leaf Litter, Lichen, Wet / Puddle Mask, Cavity Grime, Ice, Lava, Asphalt, Carbon Fibre, Paint Chips, Water Droplets

They appear in the node palette grouped by category (searchable) and their parameters get sliders, colour pickers and dropdowns automatically in the properties panel, because each op is one table row (OpDef).

Preset library (85 materials)#

The Library dropdown in the Generator header starts from a ready-made graph (one undoable step; your resolution is kept). Presets are normal graphs, so you can keep editing them. Every preset has real height variation and tiles seamlessly.

The same presets as height maps (white = surface, black = deepest) and as normal maps:

Realistic library: rock, water, foliage, ground and man-made PBR#

The Realistic category holds the Substance-style building blocks behind the photoreal presets. All of them tile, are seeded and live in uikit/procedural/realistic.rs:

Op What it makes Notable outputs
Rock Fracture angular facets, each a tilted plane with sharp cracks Colour, Height, Facet id
River Pebbles tightly packed rounded stones with gaps Colour, Height, Pebble id
Grass Blades layered, tapered, leaning and curling blades over soil Colour, Height, Blade id
Water Waves sum of directional waves (integer wave vectors, so it tiles) plus capillary ripples Colour, Height
Foam crest foam with lacework, from any height input or its own noise Mask
Bark Fissures vertically stretched plates separated by fissures Colour, Height
Soil Clumps clods, crumbs and small stones Colour, Height
Leaf Litter overlapping leaves with veins, three to four layers deep Colour, Height
Lichen ragged colonies Mask
Wet / Puddle Mask low areas of a height input fill with water Mask
Cavity Grime dirt gathering in the crevices of a height input Mask
Ice, Lava, Asphalt, Carbon Fibre, Paint Chips, Water Droplets single-purpose surfaces Lava also outputs Emissive

Rendered by the engine on a floor with parallax depth, a real sun and shadows:

Accent layers. A preset can carry a third layer (moss, foam, rust, lichen, wetness...). The accent's value is the mask: it blends its colour over the surface, drives the roughness towards a target (wet = glossy) and adds a little height. Presets built this way are normal graphs (Lerp nodes keyed by the accent), so you can rebalance or replace the accent in the node editor. wear scales the accent as well.

Preset families: Realistic Rock (granite cliff, basalt columns, limestone, sandstone, mossy boulder, lichen granite, river and wet pebbles, lava flow, frozen lake), Realistic Water (ocean swell, choppy sea, calm lake, tropical shallows, river rapids, rain puddle, droplets on glass, swamp), Realistic Nature (lawn, meadow, dry and tall wild grass, pine needles, forest floor, autumn leaves), Realistic Ground (soil, forest mud, fresh and cracked asphalt), Realistic Wood (oak, pine and birch bark) and Realistic Man-made (carbon fibre, chipped red and blue paint, rusty painted panel, mossy brick wall).

Variation: lively patterns that never repeat#

A repeated tile or a clean noise looks mechanical. The Variation class adds controlled randomness so surfaces look lived-in. Every op is seeded (a new seed is a new variation of the same material), deterministic, and keeps results seamless where its input is (uikit/procedural/variation.rs).

Node What it does Main controls
Noise Variation Perlin or Simplex noise drifts the input's brightness, hue and saturation in large soft patches, each channel with its own noise field noise kind, patch size, octaves, brightness / hue / saturation drift, contrast
Cell Variation every cell gets its own random tone, and optionally its own offset into the input (stochastic tiling). Cells are a grid, Voronoi, or the pattern's own cell ids: wire a brick / stone / tile pattern's Variation output into Cell ID and each brick varies individually cells, brightness / hue / saturation variation, texture shift, jitter
Patch Blend mixes two inputs (A, B) in organic patches shaped by Perlin / Simplex noise: clean and worn, wet and dry, moss and rock noise kind, patch size, coverage of B, edge softness
Tile Shuffle cuts the input into cells and swaps, rotates and flips them at random cells, swap chance, rotate, flip
Wave Function Collapse builds a new arrangement, of any size, whose every local neighbourhood already exists in a sample: bricks, tiles, runes... see below output cells, sample cells, pattern size (2 or 3), tone levels, symmetry, softness
Diamond-Square the classic fractal heightfield (clouds, dunes, rock relief), computed on a torus so it tiles grid (2^n), roughness (Hurst exponent), contrast, bicubic smoothing

Wave Function Collapse (overlapping model). The sample (the connected input, or a built-in brick wall when nothing is connected) is reduced to sample x sample cells and quantised into levels tone bands; every N x N window of it (optionally flipped / rotated) becomes a pattern with a weight (how often it occurs). The solver then fills a periodic output grid: it repeatedly collapses the cell with the lowest entropy to one of its remaining patterns (chosen by weight) and propagates the consequences to the neighbours, restarting with a derived seed on a contradiction (up to 14 attempts, then falling back to a random draw from the sample's tones). Because the output is periodic it tiles, and the test wave_function_collapse_only_builds_arrangements_the_sample_allows checks that every window of the result exists in the sample. The Value output is the tone band: feed it to a Gradient Map for crisp, recolourable results.

Tips: WFC needs a sample with chunky features (a few tones, features several cells wide). Thin lines vanish when the sample is reduced, so a 1 px mortar line is lost; raise Sample cells (up to 32) or pre-thicken the sample. Pattern size 3 follows the sample closely, 2 explores more. Patterns are capped at 420 so the solver stays fast (about 0.6 s extra for a 1024 px bake).

Varied presets. Seven presets show the class working (Varied category): Varied Brick Wall, Varied Cobblestone, Varied Planks, Varied Hex Tiles (each brick, stone, plank or tile gets its own tone from the pattern's cell ids, plus Simplex drift across the wall), WFC Brick Remix, Diamond-Square Badlands and Diamond-Square Moss Rock. They are normal graphs, so the Variation nodes can be rebalanced or replaced in the node editor.

2. The Output node#

Inputs, in order (older graphs keep working: new ports are appended):

Port Meaning
Color, Roughness, Metallic, Height, AO as before
Emissive colour → baked to <name>_gen_emissive_*.png, sets the material's emission map
Opacity scalar → baked into the base colour's alpha; the material switches to Cutout if it was opaque
Normal optional authored normal (OpenGL); wins over the height-derived one

Options: auto_height (default on: when Height is not connected, the height is derived from the base colour's luminance so heights are never a flat plane), normalize_height (stretches to the full 0..1 range) and height_contrast.

The generator's Output preview has a channel switcher so you can look at every baked map, not only the colour:

Height Normal
Roughness AO

3. Real depth: parallax occlusion mapping#

Before, a height map only fed the normal map, so surfaces were lit like relief but stayed geometrically flat. The renderer now does parallax occlusion mapping (POM) in the PBR shader: the view ray is marched through the height field, the UV is shifted to where it first meets the surface, and every texture (albedo, normal, ORM, emission) is sampled there. Bricks occlude their mortar, cobbles overlap their joints.

Left: depth off. Right: depth on (same maps, same lights).

How the height is stored#

The renderer has 16 fragment samplers and the PBR shader already used all of them (an SDL GPU limit), so the height lives in the alpha channel of the normal map (1 = surface, 0 = deepest). No extra texture or sampler.

  • Generator bake writes the normal map with the baked height in alpha and turns parallax on (height_scale 0.035) when the height has relief. A value you already tuned is kept.
  • External height map: in the Material panel press Pack a height map into the normal…, pick an image, and Doppio writes <material>_height_normal.png (height resampled to the normal's size) next to the material. Your original normal map is never overwritten; if the material has no normal yet, one is derived from the height first.

Controls#

Setting (.mat) Meaning
Parallax depth (height_scale) depth in UV units of the tiled texture; 0 = off, typical 0.02 – 0.06
Parallax steps (parallax_steps) maximum ray-march steps (4 – 96); the shader uses fewer when looking straight on

Notes and limits: the effect needs a normal map whose alpha holds the height (external normal maps usually have alpha 255 = flat, so nothing happens until you pack a height); grazing angles are offset-limited to avoid smearing; polygon silhouettes and shadows are not displaced (it is a texture-space technique). height_scale and parallax_steps are part of the C ABI (version 3), the .mat file (height_scale, parallax_steps) and the preview cache key.

4. Baking, repeatedly#

Baking writes <material>_gen_*.png over the same file names every time. The material preview used to key its cache on the path only, so a second bake looked unchanged. The preview now also hashes each texture's modification time and size, so every bake refreshes the preview (and any tool that rewrites a map in place does too). Covered by generator_bake_can_run_again_and_stores_height_as_real_depth.

Why a re-bake could still look unchanged. The preview's hash was right, but the engine's GPU texture cache only refreshed a file that changed on disk when its reference count was zero. The count is raised on every acquire and never drops while a map is used, so the first bake stayed on screen. The cache now reloads whenever the file's modification time moves (covered by preview_reloads_a_map_rewritten_in_place).

Purely procedural graphs also preview and bake without an engine session; only graphs that read project images need one to locate them.

5. The material preview: light, shadows and resolution#

The preview sphere now has its own sun. Under the shape / environment / exposure controls:

Control Effect
Light direction sun yaw around the subject (-180..180 degrees)
Light height sun elevation (2..89 degrees)
Light intensity sun brightness
Shadows toggles the shadow map

Agents use set_material_preview_sun (yaw, elevation, intensity, shadows). The preview renders at 768 px with the camera closer, on a brighter floor with a soft sky fill, so a material's relief, its cast shadow and its wet or dry gloss can be judged immediately. With Geometric displacement enabled the sphere is subdivided and really displaced, and its silhouette and shadows show it.

Engine fix found while building this. The directional shadow pass has no depth attachment, so whichever mesh was drawn last overwrote the others: a floor drawn after a sphere erased the sphere's shadow. The pass now uses BlendMode::Min, which keeps the nearest occluder regardless of draw order. The process-wide GPU caches (textures, procedural meshes, mesh cache) are also released when a session shuts down, so a second session no longer inherits handles from a dead device.

6. Scaling an object: keep the texture density#

A mesh's UVs are authored 1:1, so a quad scaled to twice its size used to stretch its material to twice the size too. Materials now have Scale UVs with the object (.mat key uv_object_scale, on by default, in the Material panel's UV card):

How it works: the vertex shader measures how much the model matrix stretches the mesh's tangent (U) and bitangent (V) directions and the fragment shader multiplies the tiled UV by that factor. A plane scaled 4x tiles the texture 4x, a stretched cube keeps its density on every face, and at scale 1 nothing changes (scaled_objects_keep_their_texture_density_when_uvs_follow_the_scale checks both). The same factor is used by the geometric-displacement vertex and shadow shaders, so relief stays aligned with the colour.

Case Behaviour
Scale 1 identical to before
Uniform scale the texture tiles by the scale
Non-uniform scale on a box or plane each face uses its own U / V stretch
Curved mesh with non-uniform scale the factor varies smoothly with the tangent direction, so very strong stretches can show a slight density change
Instanced draws (batched vegetation) keep the authored UVs
Material preview always shows the authored UVs (its shapes have fixed sizes)
Tiling / Offset still apply on top: the final UV is uv * tiling * objectScale + offset

Turn it off for materials whose UVs are already in world units (a world-aligned atlas, a decal). Materials written before the key existed behave like new ones (on). uv_object_scale is part of the C ABI (version 6), the .mat file, the preview cache key and the agent's material query.

7. Regenerating the images#

bash
./rebuild.sh                              # engine + Doppio (needs ImageMagick for the sheets)
./scripts/render-material-gallery.sh      # bakes all presets, renders sheets + depth comparisons
./scripts/render-variation-docs.sh        # the Variation node and preset sheets
./scripts/capture-material-docs.sh        # headless UI screenshots (generator, channels, panel)
doppio/target/release/doppio-material bake-preset "Red Brick" --out /tmp/brick   # one preset to disk
doppio/target/release/doppio-material bake-graph path/to/material.mgraph --size 2048  # time one graph

  • doppio-material bake-graph <file.mgraph> [--size N] [--out DIR] bakes an existing graph with per-stage progress timings; useful when a 2K bake looks stuck in the editor.

  • doppio-material bake-preset <name|--all> --out DIR [--size 512] [--depth 0.04] [--list] writes *_base.png, *_normal.png (height in alpha), *_orm.png, *.mat and *_flat.mat (same maps, depth off) — usable in any scene.

  • The depth renders use caffeine-render-snapshot with SNAP_FLOOR_MAT=<file.mat> SNAP_ONLY_FLOOR=1 and view preset 4.

  • The UI screenshots come from the headless driver (see headless-testing.md); the flow is caffeine-website/captures/flows/capture-material-docs.json.
